motivating_questions.content: Many experimentally and technologically relevant plasmonic systems are non-spherical, facet-dependent, alloyed or heterostructured, and surface chemistry (adsorbates, catalytic sites) can strongly affect both single-particle spectra and relaxation pathways. Existing large-scale methods either lack atomistic resolution or are computationally prohibitive for such complex geometries. A computational pipeline that decouples the single-particle spectral computation from the choice of relaxation model and that scales to very large sparse Hamiltonians is therefore needed to extend predictive hot-carrier studies to realistic, complex nanostructures. The present framework is designed to fill this gap and enable subsequent investigations of shape, composition and interface effects on steady-state hot-carrier populations.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A computational toolkit and workflow is demonstrated that integrates (i) Lanczos recursion with stochastic trace evaluation and wave-packet time evolution to obtain density of states (DOS) and Kubo-Greenwood dc conductivities, (ii) kernel polynomial method (KPM) expansions with kernels (Jackson, Lorentz) to compute DOS and Kubo conductivities to controlled resolution $ \eta $, and (iii) an exact Chebyshev polynomial Green's-function (CPGF) expansion that expresses the resolvent $\hat{\mathcal{G}}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty g_n(z)\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})$ with $g_n(z)=\tfrac{2 i^{-1}}{1+\delta_{n,0}}\tfrac{(z-i\sqrt{1-z^2})^n}{\sqrt{1-z^2}}$, allowing the evaluation of spectral quantities and the dc Kubo conductivity via finite double-sum expansions. Numerical recipes are provided for stochastic trace evaluation using random-phase vectors, Chebyshev recursion to build $\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})|r\rangle$, and a single-energy algorithm to compute $\sigma_N(\epsilon,\eta)$ on a parametric grid while storing only a small number of vectors. steps.reasoning: State the computational objectives that the toolkit must satisfy: enable computation of spectral functions (density of states, DOS) and linear-response transport (dc Kubo conductivity) in extremely large sparse tight-binding systems (millions-to-billions of orbitals) with controlled energy resolution $\eta$ (where $\eta$ denotes an energy broadening or resolution) and practical memory usage on available high-performance computing resources.

Present the Lanczos-recursion plus wave-packet time-evolution elements: use Lanczos recursion to tridiagonalize the Hamiltonian in a Lanczos basis, obtain continued-fraction representations of Green-function diagonal elements and of the spectral operator $\delta(E-\hat{H})$, and obtain time-dependent wave-packet evolution to compute the mean-square displacement $\Delta X^2(E,t)$ and hence the dc conductivity from the Kubo-Greenwood relation $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=e^2 n(E_F)\lim_{t\to\infty} \tfrac{d}{dt}\Delta X^2(E_F,t)$, where $n(E)=\tfrac{1}{V}\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})]$ is the DOS per unit volume, $\hat{V}_x$ is the velocity operator, and $e$ is the electron charge.
        (Fan et al., 2014; Foa Torres et al., 2014; Latil et al., 2004; Leconte et al., 2011)

Explain stochastic trace evaluation used with Lanczos/time-evolution: replace full traces by averages over random-phase vectors $|\varphi_{\mathrm{RP}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{j=1}^M e^{i2\pi\theta_j}|\varphi_j\rangle$ with $\theta_j$ uniform in $[0,1]$, so that $\mathrm{Tr}[\hat{O}]\approx\frac{M}{N_{\mathrm{RP}}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{RP}}}\langle\varphi_{\mathrm{RP}}^i|\hat{O}|\varphi_{\mathrm{RP}}^i\rangle$; define number of random-phase vectors $R$ (or $N_{\mathrm{RP}}$) and note that for very large Hilbert-space dimension $D$ self-averaging makes $R=1$ often sufficient.
        Iitaka and Ebisuzaki (2004)

Introduce Chebyshev polynomial expansion (KPM) for DOS and conductivity with controlled kernels: rescale the Hamiltonian spectrum to $x\in[-1,1]$, expand target functions in Chebyshev polynomials $T_n(x)$ with moments $\mu_n=\mathrm{Tr}[T_n(\tilde{H})]$, truncate at order $N$, and use damping kernels $g_n$ (e.g., Jackson kernel or Lorentz kernel) to control Gibbs oscillations; resolution scales as $\delta\epsilon_N\propto 1/N$, and for conductivity the KPM formula requires evaluation of the double-sum of conductivity moments $\Delta_{nm}=\mathrm{Tr}[\tilde{v}_x T_n(\tilde{H})\tilde{v}_x T_m(\tilde{H})]$ with complexity quadratic in $N$.
        Fig. 6
        Weisse et al., 2006

Present the exact Chebyshev-polynomial Green's-function (CPGF) expansion: define the resolvent (retarded Green function) $\hat{\mathcal{G}}(z)=(z-\hat{h})^{-1}$ with rescaled Hamiltonian $\hat{h}$ and complex energy $z=\epsilon+i\lambda$ (where $\lambda>0$ is a broadening), and state the exact Chebyshev expansion $\hat{\mathcal{G}}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} g_n(z)\,\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})$, with the coefficients
        $g_n(z)=\dfrac{2 i^{-1}}{1+\delta_{n,0}} \dfrac{\left(z-i\sqrt{1-z^2}\right)^n}{\sqrt{1-z^2}}$, where $\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})$ are operator Chebyshev polynomials defined by $\mathcal{T}_0(\hat{h})=\mathbb{I}_D,\ \mathcal{T}_1(\hat{h})=\hat{h}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{n+1}(\hat{h})=2\hat{h}\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})-\mathcal{T}_{n-1}(\hat{h})$.
        (Ferreira, 2016; Ferreira and Mucciolo, 2015)

Show how spectral and transport quantities are computed from CPGF: express the smeared DOS as $\nu(\epsilon,\lambda)=-\frac{1}{\pi D}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\mu_n$ (with moments $\mu_n=\mathrm{Tr}[\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})]$), and express the dc Kubo conductivity with finite broadening $\lambda$ as $\sigma_N(\epsilon,\lambda)=\frac{2\hbar e^2}{\pi\Omega}\sum_{n,m=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\mathrm{Im}[g_m(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\,\mathcal{V}_{nm}$ where $\mathcal{V}_{nm}=\mathrm{Tr}[\hat{v}_x\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})\hat{v}_x\mathcal{T}_m(\hat{h})]$; define $\Omega$ as sample area and $\hat{v}_x=(i/\hbar)[\hat{H},\hat{x}]$.
        (Ferreira and Mucciolo, 2015)

Give the key numerical recipes enabling large-scale feasibility: (i) stochastic trace evaluation using complex random-phase vectors to compute Chebyshev moments with cost $\mathcal{O}(D\times R\times N)$ operations for $N$ moments and $R$ random vectors, (ii) Chebyshev recursion to build $\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})|r\rangle$ by the three-term recurrence $|r\rangle_{n+1}=2\hat{h}|r\rangle_{n}-|r\rangle_{n-1}$ starting from $|r\rangle_0=|r\rangle$, and (iii) a single-energy algorithm for conductivity that constructs energy-dependent linear combinations $|\varphi_{\pm}(\epsilon,\eta)\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon+i\eta)]\,(\hat{v}_x|r_n\rangle\ \text{or}\ |\bar{r}_n\rangle)$ so that $\sigma_N(\epsilon,\eta)$ on a grid $\{\epsilon_p,\eta_q\}$ can be evaluated while storing only a few vectors rather than $2N$ vectors.
        Fig. 5

Report benchmark scaling and practical demonstrations: observe that for Lanczos-based spectral operators the practical computational scaling is $\propto D^{3/2}$ when the required resolution $\eta\approx\Delta\varepsilon$ scales with the mean level spacing $\Delta\varepsilon\propto 1/\sqrt{D}$ (so the number of recursion steps $N\propto\sqrt{D}$); note that in very large $D$ regimes self-averaging allows single-random-vector stochastic convergence (one random vector often suffices for $D\sim10^9$ up to thousands of moments), and demonstrate practical attainment of meV-scale resolution with thousands-to-tens-of-thousands of Chebyshev moments (for example $D=3.6\times10^{9}$ DOS calculation using one random vector and $N\sim15{,}000$ moments when self-averaging applies).
        Fig. 6; Fig. 7

State practical memory/compute tradeoffs and reproducible recipes: for conductivity evaluation the double-sum over moments makes storage of sequences $\{|r\rangle_n\}_{n=0}^{N-1}$ and $\{|\bar{r}\rangle_m\}_{m=0}^{N-1}$ advantageous when memory permits, otherwise use the single-energy (on-the-fly) algorithm to compute $\sigma_N(\epsilon_p,\eta_q)$ for a parametric grid storing only a small set of vectors; this recipe allows controlled computations of $\sigma$ and DOS on lattices up to billions of orbitals with specified energy resolution $\eta$.
        Fig. 5

motivating_questions.content: Real-space evaluation of spectral functions and Kubo transport in lattice models requires controllable numerical approximations that (a) converge to high energy resolution (meV-scale) where sharp resonances or Landau-level structures appear, (b) scale to system sizes large enough for self-averaging in macroscopic disorder realizations (millimetre-to-micrometre scales for moiré supercells), and (c) permit practical memory/computation usage on currently available HPC resources. Traditional exact diagonalization is infeasible beyond modest sizes; naive stochastic time evolution without optimized polynomial expansions suffers from ill-controlled broadening and high computational cost for fine resolution; and earlier polynomial-based methods either used kernels that introduce ad hoc broadening or did not provide an exact Green's-function expansion useful for transport with an explicit decoherence broadening parameter $\lambda$. There was thus a need for (i) stable Chebyshev-based Green's-function expansions and single-energy evaluation strategies, (ii) demonstrated recipes to compute conductivity moments $\mathcal{V}_{nm}=\mathrm{Tr}[\hat{v}_x T_n(\hat{h})\hat{v}_x T_m(\hat{h})]$ efficiently with limited memory, and (iii) convergence/benchmark evidence that these methods can reach experimentally relevant resolutions on systems containing millions-to-billions of atoms.

steps.reasoning: All considered clean and disordered models are stated to be “fully captured by modifications of the onsite energies” and “hopping terms between single $p_z$-orbitals per atom,” implying that the Hamiltonians are sparse tight-binding (TB = tight-binding) matrices whose dimension $D$ equals the number of orbitals (sites) in the lattice.

A first scalable framework is built from the Kubo–Greenwood (KG = Kubo–Greenwood) linear-response formalism written as a trace formula for the real part of the conductivity $\mathfrak{R}[\sigma(\omega)]$: $\mathfrak{R}[\sigma(\omega)]=\frac{2\pi e^{2}\hbar}{V}\int dE \frac{f(E)-f(E+\hbar\omega)}{\hbar\omega}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\hat{V}_x\delta(E-\hat{H})\hat{V}_x\delta(E+\hbar\omega-\hat{H})\right]$, where $e$ is electronic charge, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, $V$ is system volume, $f(E)$ is the Fermi function, $\hat{H}$ is the Hamiltonian operator, $\hat{V}_x$ is the velocity operator along $x$, and $\delta(\cdot)$ is the Dirac delta of an operator.

Using the identity $\delta(E+\hbar\omega-\hat{H})=\frac{1}{2\pi\hbar}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dt\, e^{i(E+\hbar\omega-\hat{H})t/\hbar}$, the conductivity is rewritten into a time-dependent trace involving $\hat{V}_x(t)$ (Heisenberg picture) and $\delta(E-\hat{H})$, leading to $\mathfrak{R}(\sigma(\omega))=e^{2}\int dt\, e^{i\omega t}\int dE\, \frac{f(E)-f(E+\hbar\omega)}{\hbar\omega} n(E)\langle \hat{V}_x(t)\hat{V}_x(0)\rangle_E$, where the density of states per volume is defined as $n(E)=\frac{1}{V}\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})]$ and the energy-resolved expectation is $\langle\hat{A}\rangle_E=\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})\hat{A}]/\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})]$.

Taking the dc limit $\omega\to 0$ and using $\lim_{\omega\to 0}\frac{f(E)-f(E+\hbar\omega)}{\hbar\omega}=\delta(E-E_F)$ (with $E_F$ the Fermi energy), the dc conductivity becomes $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=e^{2} n(E_F)\int dt\, \langle \hat{V}_x(t)\hat{V}_x(0)\rangle_{E_F}$.

Defining the mean quadratic displacement (MSD = mean square displacement) $\Delta X^{2}(E,t)=\langle(\hat{X}(t)-\hat{X}(0))^{2}\rangle_E$ and noting the relationship $\frac{d^{2}}{dt^{2}}\Delta X^{2}(E,t)=C(E,t)$ where $C(E,t)$ is a (symmetrized) velocity autocorrelation, the dc conductivity is written in the long-time limit as $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=e^{2} n(E_F)\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{d}{dt}\Delta X^{2}(E_F,t)$, which is the wave-packet-evolution implementation target formula.

A practical wave-packet-evolution estimator is given: with time-evolution operator $\hat{U}(t)=e^{-i\hat{H}t/\hbar}$, $\Delta X^2(E,t)=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}\left[[\hat{X},\hat{U}]^\dagger\delta(E-\hat{H})[\hat{X},\hat{U}(t)]\right]}{\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})]}$; therefore both numerator and denominator require traces involving $\delta(E-\hat{H})$.

The trace is made scalable by the stochastic trace evaluation (STE = stochastic trace evaluation) replacing $\mathrm{Tr}[\delta(E-\hat{H})]$ with averages over random-phase (RP = random-phase) vectors $|\varphi_{\mathrm{RP}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{j=1}^{M}e^{i2\pi\theta_j}|\varphi_j\rangle$, where $\theta_j\in[0,1]$ is random and $|\varphi_j\rangle$ is a localized orbital basis; it is stated that for large enough systems “the average over a few random phases is usually sufficient.” (Iitaka and Ebisuzaki, 2004)

Lanczos recursion is introduced as the scalable way to evaluate matrix elements of resolvents $(E+i\eta-\hat{H}')^{-1}$ as continued fractions after tridiagonalizing the TB Hamiltonian into a Lanczos basis, so that a few thousand recursion coefficients can replace the original Hamiltonian size for the purposes of evaluating $\delta(E-\hat{H})$ with resolution parameter $\eta$.

A computational scaling statement is made for this Lanczos+STE approach: “By construction, the total number of operations is given by $N\times D\times R$,” where $N$ is the number of matrix–vector multiplications (recursive steps), $D$ is Hamiltonian dimension, and $R$ is number of random vectors; furthermore, near the Dirac point of pristine graphene the level spacing scales as $\Delta\varepsilon\propto 1/\sqrt{D}$, and “optimal resolution requires $\eta\approx \Delta\varepsilon$,” giving $N\propto \sqrt{D}$ and hence an overall $D^{3/2}$ scaling for the spectral operator evaluation in that regime.

A second family of scalable methods is then presented: Chebyshev polynomial expansion approaches, described as having “numerical convergence [that] can be controlled by increasing the number of polynomial moments” and by kernel choices, avoiding “ad hoc numerical broadening.” Two main variants are detailed: the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM = kernel polynomial method) and the Chebyshev Polynomial Green's Function method (CPGF = Chebyshev polynomial Green's function). (Weisse et al., 2006; Ferreira and Mucciolo, 2015)

For KPM, the Chebyshev polynomials of the first kind are defined as $T_n(x)=\cos(n\arccos(x))$ on $x\in[-1,1]$ with recursion $T_0(x)=1$, $T_1(x)=x$, $T_{n+1}(x)=2xT_n(x)-T_{n-1}(x)$. The DOS (density of states) is expressed as $\rho(E)=\frac{1}{D}\mathrm{Tr}\,\delta(E-\hat{H})$, and after rescaling to $\epsilon\in[-1,1]$ the KPM DOS approximation is written as $\rho_{\mathrm{KPM}}(\epsilon)=\frac{2}{D\pi\sqrt{1-\epsilon^{2}}}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\frac{g_{n}}{1+\delta_{n,0}}\mu_n T_n(\epsilon)$, with moments $\mu_n=\mathrm{Tr}\,T_n(\widetilde{H})$, $\widetilde{H}=\hat{H}/W$ (for symmetric spectrum), $W$ the half-bandwidth, and $g_n$ a kernel (e.g. Jackson) to damp Gibbs oscillations.
The resolution control for KPM is stated as “usually $N\propto W/\eta$” where $\eta$ is the desired energy resolution (broadening scale), hence larger $N$ is required for finer energy resolution.

For the KPM dc conductivity, the text uses the zero-temperature Kubo formula $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}(E)=\frac{\pi g_s \hbar e^2}{\Omega}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\hat{v}_x\delta(E-\hat{H})\hat{v}_x\delta(E-\hat{H})\right]$, where $\hat{v}_x=(i/\hbar)[\hat{H},\hat{x}]$ is the velocity operator component, $g_s=2$ is spin degeneracy, and $\Omega$ is sample area. The KPM expansion is given as $\sigma_{\mathrm{KPM}}(\epsilon)=\frac{2 g_s \hbar e^2}{\pi\Omega(1-\epsilon^2)}\sum_{n,m=0}^{N-1}\Delta_{nm}\left[T_{n+m}(\epsilon)+T_{|n-m|}(\epsilon)\right]$ with $\Delta_{nm}$ involving traces $\mathrm{Tr}\left[\widetilde{v}_x T_n(\widetilde{H})\widetilde{v}_x T_m(\widetilde{H})\right]$ and kernel coefficients; it is explicitly noted that conductivity evaluation is “more demanding” because the cost is “quadratic in $N$,” unlike DOS which is linear in $N$.

For the CPGF method, the Green function is defined for rescaled complex energy $z=\epsilon+i\lambda$ (with $\lambda>0$ a broadening parameter) as $\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon+i\lambda)=\sum_m \frac{|m\rangle\langle m|}{\epsilon+i\lambda-\epsilon_m}$, where $\epsilon_m$ and $|m\rangle$ are eigenvalues/eigenvectors of the rescaled Hamiltonian $\hat{h}$. Using a stated identity expanding $e^{-ixz}$ into Chebyshev polynomials and Bessel functions, the Green function is derived (by Laplace transform and analytic continuation $s\to -iz$) into an exact Chebyshev operator expansion $\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon+i\lambda)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} g_n(\epsilon+i\lambda)\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})$, where $\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})$ are operator Chebyshev polynomials obeying $\mathcal{T}_0(\hat{h})=\mathbb{I}_D$, $\mathcal{T}_1(\hat{h})=\hat{h}$, $\mathcal{T}_{n+1}(\hat{h})=2\hat{h}\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})-\mathcal{T}_{n-1}(\hat{h})$, and $g_n(z)=\frac{2 i^{-1}}{1+\delta_{n,0}}\frac{(z-i\sqrt{1-z^2})^n}{\sqrt{1-z^2}}$. (Tal-Ezer and Kosloff, 1984; Gradshteyn and Ryzhik, 2007)

From this Green-function expansion, the (disorder-averaged) smeared DOS is defined as $\nu(\epsilon,\lambda)=-\frac{1}{\pi D}\mathrm{TrIm}\,\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon+i\lambda)$, yielding the finite-$N$ approximation $\nu_N(\epsilon,\lambda)=-\frac{1}{\pi D}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\mu_n$, where $\mu_n$ are Chebyshev moments as in KPM; the broadening is unambiguously tied to resolution via $\eta=\lambda W$ (with $W$ the half-bandwidth).

The CPGF dc conductivity is given as $\sigma(\epsilon,\lambda)=\frac{2\hbar e^2}{\pi\Omega}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\overline{\mathrm{Im}\,\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon+i\lambda)\hat{v}_x\mathrm{Im}\,\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon+i\lambda)\hat{v}_x}\right]$, and the finite-$N$ expansion is stated as $\sigma_N(\epsilon,\lambda)=\frac{2\hbar e^2}{\pi\Omega}\sum_{n,m=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\mathrm{Im}[g_m(\epsilon+i\lambda)]\mathcal{V}_{nm}$ with $\mathcal{V}_{nm}=\mathrm{Tr}\left[\hat{v}_x\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})\hat{v}_x\mathcal{T}_m(\hat{h})\right]$, and it is again emphasized that conductivity is more demanding because it involves $N^2$ moments.

For efficient calculation of Chebyshev moments, STE is presented in a general form: $\mu_n\approx \frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\langle r|\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})|r\rangle$, where $|r\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{D}\xi_i|i\rangle$ are complex random vectors with $\langle\langle\xi_i\rangle\rangle=0$ and $\langle\langle\xi_i^*\xi_j\rangle\rangle=\delta_{ij}$; the per-moment operation count is stated as $\mathcal{O}(D\times R)$.

A practical recursion-based vector generation scheme is provided: define $|r\rangle_m=\mathcal{T}_m(\hat{h})|r\rangle$ so that $|r\rangle_{m+1}=2\hat{h}|r\rangle_m-|r\rangle_{m-1}$; define auxiliary vectors $|\bar{r}\rangle=\hat{v}_x|r\rangle$ and $|\bar{r}\rangle_n=\mathcal{T}_n(\hat{h})|\bar{r}\rangle$ with the same recursion. Then conductivity moments can be assembled from overlaps $\mathcal{V}_{nm}(r)={}_n\langle \bar{r}|\hat{v}_x|r\rangle_m$ and averaged over $R$ random vectors.

A memory-aware “single-energy algorithm” is described for evaluating $\sigma_N(\epsilon_p,\eta_q)$ on a grid of energies $\{\epsilon_p\}$ and broadenings $\{\eta_q\}$ without storing all $2N$ recursion vectors: represent $\sigma_N(\epsilon_p,\eta_q)=\frac{2\hbar e^2}{\pi\Omega R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\langle \varphi_-^{(r)}(\epsilon_p,\eta_q)|\varphi_+^{(r)}(\epsilon_p,\eta_q)\rangle$, where $|\varphi_+^{(r)}\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon_p+i\eta_q)]\hat{v}_x|r_n\rangle$ and $|\varphi_-^{(r)}\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\mathrm{Im}[g_n(\epsilon_p+i\eta_q)]|\bar{r}_n\rangle$, enabling iterative computation “with only a few vectors stored in memory.”

The framework is explicitly demonstrated as enabling calculations on extremely large systems: it is stated that the single-energy approach allows treatment of “very large TB systems, in excess of a billion atoms $(D=3.6\times 10^9)$, with high resolution,” and earlier the chapter similarly emphasizes that these polynomial methods “enable the accurate determination of linear response functions in disordered lattices containing billions of sites.”

motivating_questions.content: Accurate evaluation of spectral and linear-response transport properties for disordered and strained 2D materials at experimentally relevant system sizes is hindered by the unfavorable scaling of exact diagonalization and by uncontrolled numerical broadening in small-system approaches. Prior large-scale approaches lacked a unified, controlled prescription that (i) quantifies resolution ($\eta$) versus polynomial order ($N$) tradeoffs, (ii) exploits stochastic trace evaluation suitable for sparse TB Hamiltonians of dimension $D\gtrsim10^7$–$10^9$, and (iii) combines time-domain Kubo formulas (wave-packet evolution) with Chebyshev-based spectral methods to compute longitudinal and transverse conductivities with controlled errors. Practically, researchers needed algorithms that (a) deliver meV energy resolution for DOS and conductivity in realistic disordered samples, (b) quantify convergence and stochastic errors (dependence on number $R$ of random vectors), and (c) operate under realistic memory constraints when computing $N^2$ conductivity moments. The presented framework addresses these numerical bottlenecks by prescribing recursion-based moment generation, stochastic trace sampling, kernel choices, and memory-aware single-energy reconstruction algorithms.

The low-energy graphene model with Rashba SOC parameter $\lambda_{R}$ and Kane-Mele SOC parameter $\lambda_{\mathrm{KM}}$, projected to a single valley ($\tau_{z}=+1$), separates into two decoupled subspaces labelled by the spin-pseudospin winding index $\chi=\pm1$, each described by the projected Hamiltonian
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{k},\chi}=\chi\frac{\lambda_{R}}{2}+\begin{pmatrix}
      -\hbar v_{\mathrm{gr}}k & -\tfrac{1}{2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{KM}}+\chi\lambda_{R})\\[4pt]
      -\tfrac{1}{2}(\lambda_{\mathrm{KM}}+\chi\lambda_{R}) & +\hbar v_{\mathrm{gr}}k
      \end{pmatrix},
      $$
      with $v_{\mathrm{gr}}$ the bare graphene velocity and $k=|\boldsymbol{k}|$. The cone $\chi$ has effective gap magnitude $|\Delta_{\chi}|=|\lambda_{R}+\chi\lambda_{\mathrm{KM}}|$, eigenvalues
      $$
      E_{\chi,\pm}=\chi\frac{\lambda_{R}}{2}\pm\varepsilon_{\chi},\qquad
      \varepsilon_{\chi}=\sqrt{(\hbar v_{\mathrm{gr}}k)^{2}+\frac{\Delta_{\chi}^{2}}{4}},
      $$
      and spin and pseudospin textures
      $$
      \langle\mathfrak{s}\rangle_{\chi,\pm}=\pm\chi\,\rho_{\chi}\,\hat{\varphi},\qquad
      \langle\boldsymbol{\sigma}\rangle_{\chi,\pm}=\pm\rho_{\chi}\,\hat{k},
      $$
      with $\rho_{\chi}=\hbar v_{\mathrm{gr}}k/\varepsilon_{\chi}$, where $\hat{k}$ is the radial pseudospin direction and $\hat{\varphi}=\hat{z}\times\hat{k}$ the azimuthal spin helicity direction. These closed-form spectral and texture expressions define how Rashba and Kane-Mele SOC combine to set effective masses, band ordering and helical textures in each $\chi$ cone.

Adopt the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM) to expand the Green's function in Chebyshev polynomials with the Jackson kernel to suppress Gibbs oscillations; denote the Chebyshev expansion order by $M$, the total single-particle bandwidth by $\Delta E$, and the resulting numerical Jackson spectral broadening at the band centre by $\eta_{\mathrm{KPM}}\approx\pi\Delta E/M$, which links the chosen expansion order $M$ to the effective energy broadening $\eta_{\mathrm{KPM}}$.

Introduce an energy-filtering technique (implemented within KPM) that allows reaching a numerical Jackson spectral broadening of order $\eta_{\mathrm{KPM}}\sim1\ \mathrm{meV}$ using Chebyshev expansion order $M\approx800$ for bandwidth $\Delta E$ typical of the graphene tight-binding model, enabling calculations with fine energy resolution at the meV scale while keeping the polynomial order computationally tractable on very large lattices.

Demonstrate scalability: deploy the energy-filtered KPM implementation on graphene systems of microscopic dimensions (system area $\sim28\ \mu\mathrm{m}^{2}$ corresponding to of order $10^{9}$ atoms), thereby enabling non-perturbative computation of both Fermi-surface and Fermi-sea transport contributions at the meV energy scale in micron-size disordered graphene samples; the method thus affords the system sizes necessary to avoid spurious finite-size effects when resolving Rashba pseudogap phenomena.

$$
where $\eta(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{F}})$ is the KPM numerical broadening at the Fermi energy, $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant, and the numerical prefactor 1.84 arises from the detailed Chebyshev/Jackson expansion and numerical evaluation of the relevant double-sum expression; this relation is used to interpret transport velocities and quasiparticle lifetimes in the simulations.

premises.content: A nine-orbital-per-site orthogonal tight-binding (TB) electronic-structure model for hexagonal-close-packed ruthenium (Ru) was parameterized by fitting TB band energies to density-functional-theory (DFT) band-structure data (training set: seven hcp structures with varying lattice parameters and 40 k-points each), using a cost that weighted bands within $\pm 3\,$eV of the Fermi energy most heavily. The TB model includes 5s, 5p, and 4d orbitals (total 9 orbitals per Ru site), on-site energies $h_{\kappa,i}$ that depend on a local site density $\rho_i$ via $h_{\kappa,i}=a_{\kappa}+b_{\kappa}\rho_i^{2/3}+c_{\kappa}\rho_i^{4/3}+d_{\kappa}\rho_i^{2}$, and two-center Slater–Koster hopping integrals of the form $P_{\gamma}(R)=(e_{\gamma}+f_{\gamma}R)\exp(-g_{\gamma}^2 R)F_c(R)$ with a cutoff radius $R_c=8.731\,$Å and $F_c(R)$ a smooth cutoff function. The fitted model reproduces DFT electronic bands near the Fermi energy and the cohesive-energy versus volume curve (Birch–Murnaghan fits for $V_0$, $E_{\mathrm{coh}}$, and $B$), yielding lattice parameters and bulk elastic properties in good agreement with DFT and experiment for the parameterization used.

Conductivity computation framework: the energy-resolved conductivity tensor components $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(E)$ are given by the Kubo–Greenwood expression $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(E)=\dfrac{2\pi\hbar e^{2}}{\Omega}\mathrm{Tr}\!\left[\hat{v}_\alpha \delta(E-\hat{H}) \hat{v}_\beta \delta(E-\hat{H})\right]$, where $\Omega$ is the system volume, $\hat{H}$ is the TB Hamiltonian, and $\hat{v}_\alpha$ is the velocity operator defined by $\hat{v}_\alpha=\dfrac{i}{\hbar}[\hat{H},\hat{x}_\alpha]$ for Cartesian coordinate $\alpha$.
Eq. (4)
Eq. (5)

To evaluate the trace efficiently for systems with large Hilbert-space dimension (number of sites $N$ times 9 orbitals per site), the stochastic truncated-basis approximation is used: the trace is estimated with $R$ random vectors $|R_r\rangle$ of length $9N$, giving $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(E)\approx \dfrac{2\pi\hbar e^{2}}{\Omega}\dfrac{1}{R}\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}\langle R_r|\hat{v}_\alpha\delta(E-\hat{H})\hat{v}_\beta\delta(E-\hat{H})|R_r\rangle$, which reduces computational cost by replacing the full trace with an average over random probes.
Eq. (6)

The delta operator $\delta(E-\hat{H})$ is approximated via a Chebyshev (kernel polynomial method, KPM) expansion: define rescaled energy $\varepsilon=(E-E_m)/\Delta E$ and rescaled Hamiltonian $\hat{h}=(\hat{H}-E_m)/\Delta E$, where $E_m$ is the band midpoint and $\Delta E$ is the half-bandwidth; the KPM approximations for the vectors $|\Psi_{\alpha,r}(E)\rangle=\delta(E-\hat{H})\hat{v}_{\alpha}|R_r\rangle$ and $|\Phi_{\beta,r}(E)\rangle=\hat{v}_\beta\delta(E-\hat{H})|R_r\rangle$ are written using Chebyshev polynomials $T_n$ and kernel coefficients $g_n$ as
$|\Psi_{\alpha,r}(E)\rangle=\dfrac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}}\left[g_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N_T-1} g_n T_n(\varepsilon) T_n(\hat{h})\hat{v}_\alpha\right]|R_r\rangle$
and
$|\Phi_{\beta,r}(E)\rangle=\dfrac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^{2}}}\left[g_0+\sum_{n=1}^{N_T-1} g_n T_n(\varepsilon) \hat{v}_\beta T_n(\hat{h})\right]|R_r\rangle$,
enabling recursive evaluation of the Chebyshev terms via sparse Hamiltonian–vector products.
[9]
Eqs. (10) and (11)

The Jackson kernel is used to define the kernel coefficients $g_n$ that damp Gibbs oscillations and improve convergence; the explicit Jackson kernel functional form for $g_n$ is applied in the Chebyshev expansions to yield stable approximations of $\delta(E-\hat{H})$ with finite-order truncation $N_T$.
Eq. (12)

Choice of truncation and stochastic parameters: $N_T=242$ Chebyshev moments were used everywhere, together with the Jackson kernel; for in-plane conductivity components ($\sigma_{xx}$ and $\sigma_{yy}$) a stochastic trace with $36$ random vectors was sufficient for convergence (for $\sigma_{zz}$ $108$ random vectors were used); convergence with respect to the number of random vectors was assessed by statistical $t'$-tests at each energy and by ensuring that increases in random vectors produced statistically indistinguishable conductivity spectra.

Practical computational scaling and system sizes: because the TB Hamiltonian is sparse and the KPM evaluation uses repeated sparse matrix–vector multiplications, the computational cost scales approximately linearly with system size for fixed $N_T$ and $R$; as implemented, this enabled simulations of thin films containing up to $\sim 3.8\times 10^5$ atomic sites, with in-plane transport lengths of order $160\,$nm, film widths $\sim 5\,$nm, and thicknesses approaching $5\,$nm, with a KPM rhombohedral bulk supercell containing 327,680 atoms used for bulk resistivity calculations.

Role of $N_T$ as an effective inelastic broadening: for ballistic or quasi-ballistic systems the computed conductivity depends on the number of Chebyshev moments; here $N_T$ was chosen so that the bulk basal-plane resistivity computed with KPM matches the experimental room-temperature basal-plane resistivity $\rho_{RT}=7.6\,\mu\Omega\,$cm, effectively using the Chebyshev truncation to mimic an inelastic relaxation process that mixes states within an energy window of order $\Delta E/N_T$.
Sec. III and Eq. (12)

Comparison to Boltzmann-Transport-Equation (BTE) calculations: independent BTE calculations in the single-relaxation-time approximation were performed using the BTE conductivity expression $\sigma_{\mu\nu}=\dfrac{2e^2\tau}{N_k V_{\mathrm{cell}}}\sum_{\lambda,\vec{k}} (\vec{e}_\mu\cdot\vec{v}_{\lambda\vec{k}})(\vec{e}_\nu\cdot\vec{v}_{\lambda\vec{k}})\left(-\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial\epsilon}\right)_{\epsilon=E_\lambda(\vec{k})}$ with relaxation time $\tau=9.45\,$fs chosen to reproduce the experimental room-temperature basal-plane resistivity; the KPM bulk resistivity and anisotropy agree closely with the BTE results using this $\tau$, validating the KPM transport calculations against an independent transport framework.

A concrete, local tight-binding Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian on the two-dimensional Ammann–Beenker (8-fold symmetric) quasicrystalline tiling is defined and shown to realize a higher-order topological superconducting phase with eight Majorana zero modes localized at the octagonal sample corners. The Hamiltonian is given in real space by
      $$
      \mathcal{H}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{\Psi}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathcal{H}_{j}\mathbf{\Psi}_{j}+\sum_{\langle j,k\rangle}\mathbf{\Psi}_{j}^{\dagger}\mathcal{H}_{jk}\mathbf{\Psi}_{k},
      $$
      with Nambu spinor $\mathbf{\Psi}_{j}^{\dagger}=(\psi_{j,\uparrow}^{\dagger},\psi_{j,\uparrow},\psi_{j,\downarrow}^{\dagger},\psi_{j,\downarrow})$ and onsite term
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{j}=\mu\,\sigma_{z}\tau_{z},
      $$
      normal- and pairing-hopping terms for a $p\pm ip$ bilayer
      $$
      \mathcal{H}_{jk}=\tfrac{t}{2}\sigma_{z}\tau_{z}+\tfrac{\Delta}{2i}\big[\cos(\alpha_{jk})\sigma_{z}\tau_{x}+\sin(\alpha_{jk})\sigma_{z}\tau_{y}\big],
      $$
      and an edge-mass perturbation
      $$
      \mathcal{V}=\sum_{\langle j,k\rangle}\mathbf{\Psi}_{j}^{\dagger}\bigg(\tfrac{V}{2}\sigma_{y}\tau_{0}\cos(4\alpha_{jk})\bigg)\mathbf{\Psi}_{k}.
      $$
      Here $\tau_{i}$ and $\sigma_{i}$ are Pauli matrices in particle-hole and spin space, $\alpha_{jk}$ is the bond angle, and $\mu,t,\Delta,V$ are real parameters. The model obeys particle-hole symmetry $\mathcal{P}=\tau_{x}\sigma_{0}\mathbb{1}K$, an in-plane mirror $M=\tau_{0}\sigma_{z}\mathbb{1}$, and, for an 8-fold symmetric finite patch, an on-site rotation $C_{8}=\exp\big(-i\frac{\pi}{8}\sigma_{0}\tau_{z}\big)\mathcal{R}$ that permutes sites by rotation $\mathcal{R}$. For parameter choices $t=\Delta=1$, $\mu=-1.7$ and $V=1$ the edge states are gapped and a single Majorana zero mode appears localized at each of the eight octagon corners; these localized zero-energy states are separated from other states by an energy gap.

The final expressions are
      $$
      \frac{\delta^{2} F}{\delta \theta_{i}^{2}} = 4 \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} \operatorname{Tr}\!\big[\Sigma^{i(1)}\left(\beta_{m}\otimes\alpha_{m}\right)^{T}\big] + 4\Big[\sum_{m=1}^{M-2}\langle\beta_{m}\Sigma^{i(0)}\Gamma_{m}^{i}\rangle + \sum_{m=0}^{M-3}\langle\tilde{\Gamma}_{m}^{i}\Sigma^{i(0)}\alpha_{m}\rangle\Big],
      $$
      $$
      \frac{\delta^{2} F}{\delta \theta_{i}\delta\theta_{j}} = 4\Big[\sum_{m=1}^{M-2}\langle\beta_{m}\Sigma^{j(0)}\Gamma_{m}^{i}\rangle + \sum_{m=0}^{M-3}\langle\tilde{\Gamma}_{m}^{i}\Sigma^{j(0)}\alpha_{m}\rangle\Big],
      $$
      where $\alpha_m$ and $\beta_m$ are Chebyshev-polynomial expansion vectors defined by the recursions: $\alpha_0 = r$ (a random column vector of dimension $N$, the Hamiltonian matrix size), $\alpha_1 = A r$, $\alpha_m = 2 A \alpha_{m-1} - \alpha_{m-2}$ for $m\ge 2$; $\beta_{M-1}=\beta_M=0$, and for $m = M-2,\dots,1$: $\beta_m = c_{m+1} r^\dagger + 2 \beta_{m+1} A - \beta_{m+2}$, $\beta_0 = \frac12 (c_1 r^\dagger + 2 \beta_1 A - \beta_2)$. The coefficients $c_m = \frac{1}{\pi}(2-\delta_{0m}) g_m \int_{-1}^{1} dx \frac{T_m(x) f(x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, where $f(x)=-T\log(1+e^{-\beta(x-\mu)})$ is the Fermi function at temperature $T$ and chemical potential $\mu$, $T_m(x)$ are Chebyshev polynomials, and $g_m$ is the Jackson kernel $g_m = \frac{(M-m+1)\cos\frac{\pi m}{M+1}+\sin\frac{\pi m}{M+1}\cot\frac{\pi}{M+1}}{M+1}$. steps.reasoning:
Define the tight-binding model used as follows: localized orbitals $\phi_i$ inhabit a $d$-dimensional lattice with integer site indices $i\in\mathbb{Z}^d$, and the hopping matrix elements between orbitals are denoted $t_{ij}$; the model Hamiltonian matrix elements are denoted $H_{ij}$ and are constructed from these $t_{ij}$.
[14]

Introduce the configuration space $\Omega$ as the compact set of all local environments experienced by an orbital in the infinite, possibly incommensurate, layered stack; specifically for relative in-plane shifts between layers, $\Omega$ is the compact two-dimensional space of all relative shifts (offsets) between layer unit cells, and an individual configuration is denoted $\omega\in\Omega$.
[14]

For each configuration $\omega\in\Omega$, construct a finite-radius real-space disk centered at a chosen origin; denote the disk radius by $R$ (in length units), and define the finite-radius configuration Hamiltonian $H^{\omega}$ as the sparse tight-binding Hamiltonian obtained by including orbitals within the disk and all nonzero hopping matrix elements $t_{ij}$ that connect orbitals whose real-space separation lies within the prescribed hopping range; thus $H^{\omega}_{ij}=t_{ij}$ for those orbital pairs included and $H^{\omega}_{ij}=0$ otherwise.

State the controllable finite-size error property: observables computed from the finite-radius Hamiltonian $H^{\omega}$ converge to their infinite-system limits as the disk radius $R$ increases, with the finite-size and edge errors decaying exponentially with $R$ (so error can be made arbitrarily small by choosing sufficiently large $R$); this underlies the ability to remove finite-size artifacts in a controlled fashion.
[16]

Define the global electronic density of states (EDoS) $g(\epsilon)$ and its decomposition into local electronic density of states (LEDoS) contributions $g_x(\epsilon)$ at orbital index $x$ by the spectral expansion
$$
g(\epsilon)=\sum_x g_x(\epsilon)=\sum_{x}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}\delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_s)|\phi_s(x)|^2,
$$
where $s$ indexes eigenstates, $N$ is the number of eigenstates in the finite system, $\epsilon_s$ are eigenenergies, $x$ indexes orbitals, and $\phi_s(x)$ are the eigenstate amplitudes on orbital $x$ (this is the explicit form of the LEDoS decomposition used).

Explain the numerical evaluation of spectral observables via the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM): to approximate spectral functions of $H^{\omega}$, first rescale $H^{\omega}$ so that its spectrum lies in the interval $[-1,1]$, then expand spectral functions in the orthogonal Chebyshev polynomial basis $\{T_i\}$ (where $T_i$ denotes the $i$-th Chebyshev polynomial) and truncate the expansion to obtain a controlled approximation with tunable resolution and smoothing parameters determined by the expansion order and kernel choice.
[31]

State the practical assembly procedure for $H^{\omega}$ used in the implementation: determine all relevant hopping index pairs $(i,j)$ by searching for orbital pairs within the hopping range; for each sampled $\omega$ displace the layers according to $\omega$ and compute the nonzero hopping matrix elements $H^{\omega}_{ij}$ for the finite disk; these sparse matrix elements are then used directly in KPM evaluations of local and global spectral observables for that configuration.

Describe how material specificity and parameter-free Hamiltonians are obtained: use ab initio density-functional calculations followed by Wannier projections to produce tight-binding parameters $t_{ij}$ without adjustable fitting parameters (so the Hamiltonians are parameter-free in the sense of being derived from first principles), and employ those Wannier-derived tight-binding models as the input $t_{ij}$ used in assembling each $H^{\omega}$.
[18]

Explain inclusion of external electromagnetic fields and local defects: external magnetic fields are incorporated via a Peierls substitution (phases on hopping matrix elements) or by on-site energy terms for electric fields; physical defects (vacancies, ripples, edges) are included by augmenting the definition of $\Omega$ with additional disorder degrees of freedom representing the local defect configurations and by modifying the corresponding $H^{\omega}$ entries accordingly.

Explain computational workflow and scalability: sample many independent configurations $\omega\in\Omega$ and evaluate each $H^{\omega}$ and its KPM expansion independently (this is an embarrassingly parallel outer loop over $\omega$); within each $H^{\omega}$ KPM evaluation, exploit sparse matrix-vector operations and optimized multi-threaded linear algebra libraries to obtain efficient inner-loop performance; the implementation reported uses MVAPICH for distributed parallelism and Intel MKL for optimized sparse matrix-vector operations, resulting in computational efficiency favorable relative to brute-force DFT supercell calculations when sampling many twist angles and configurations.
[31]

Summarize the method as a whole: replace Bloch-$\mathbf{k}$ sampling (the Brillouin zone) by sampling the compact configuration space $\Omega$ of relative shifts and other local disorder degrees of freedom; for each sampled $\omega$ assemble finite-radius sparse $H^{\omega}$ from ab initio Wannier-derived hoppings; evaluate local and global spectral quantities via KPM with controlled finite-radius convergence; and parallelize over independent $\omega$ samples to obtain a parameter-free, material-specific computational framework applicable to arbitrary (including incommensurate) twist angles.
[17]

motivating_questions.content: In modeling electronic structure of twisted multilayer 2D systems, researchers needed a method that (i) is parameter-free in the sense of using ab initio-derived tight-binding rather than heuristic fitting; (ii) applies to arbitrary (including incommensurate) twist angles where no Brillouin zone exists; (iii) gives local observables (LEDoS) and global spectral functions with quantifiable control of finite-size and edge effects; and (iv) allows inclusion of external fields and local defects within the same framework. Prior techniques either (a) used periodic supercells derived from commensurate approximations and hence could only access special discrete angles with large computational cost, or (b) used low-energy continuum models that lacked full material-specific orbital content and could not handle arbitrary disorder or wide energy windows. Consequently, there was no practical ab initio-tight-binding workflow that both controlled finite-size errors and sampled the infinite incommensurate configurations needed to produce converged, material-specific DOS and related observables across arbitrary twist angles. The conclusion presents a concrete method to fill this gap by: replacing Bloch-$\mathbf{k}$ sampling with sampling over the compact configuration space $\Omega$, assembling finite-radius sparse Hamiltonians $H^{\omega}$ that converge to the infinite limit, and using KPM to compute spectral observables efficiently.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: The Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM) using Chebyshev polynomial expansion of site-resolved local density of states $\rho_i(E)$ combined with Jackson damping factors $g_n$ and the geometrical averaging diagnostic $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)$ versus arithmetic average $\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$ provides an operational and computationally feasible scheme to diagnose extended versus localized single-particle states in disordered bilayer graphene on lattices up to $L=8\times10^4$ sites. Practically, the method uses a rescaled Hamiltonian $\tilde{H}$ with eigenvalues in $[-1,1]$, moments $\mu_n=\frac{1}{D}\langle i|T_n(\tilde{H})|i\rangle$ and stochastic trace evaluation for $\mu_n'=\frac{1}{D}\mathrm{Tr}[T_n(\tilde{H})]$, requires expansion order scaling approximately as $N\sim L^2$ to maintain resolution, and employs finite-size scaling of $R(E)=\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)/\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$ (computed with $K_r=15$ disorder realizations and $K_s=15$ sampled sites per realization) to control system-size effects; these computational choices yield stable, convergent results for the localization diagnostics reported.

steps.reasoning: Define the physical model and the target spectral quantity: the tight-binding Hamiltonian $H$ for Bernal-stacked bilayer graphene with nearest-neighbor in-plane hopping $t$, inter-layer hopping $t_{\perp}$, and on-site energies $\epsilon_{m,i}^{a}$ and $\epsilon_{m,i}^{b}$ sampled independently from a uniform distribution in the interval $\left[-\frac{W}{2},\frac{W}{2}\right]$; the local density of states (LDOS) at lattice site $i$ and energy $E$ is $\rho_{i}(E)=\sum_{n} |\langle i|E_{n}\rangle|^{2}\delta(E-E_{n})$, where $|E_{n}\rangle$ are eigenvectors of $H$ and $E_{n}$ their eigenvalues, and the system Hilbert-space dimension is $D$.

Introduce the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM) framework used to compute LDOS without explicit diagonalization: rescale the Hamiltonian to $\tilde{H}$ by an affine transformation so that all eigenvalues of $\tilde{H}$ lie in the interval $[-1,1]$; expand $\rho_{i}(E)$ in Chebyshev polynomials $T_{n}(E)$ as
$$
\rho_{i}(E)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-E^{2}}}\Big[\mu_{0}+2\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mu_{n}T_{n}(E)\Big],
$$
where the Chebyshev moment coefficients are $\mu_{n}=\int_{-1}^{1}\rho_{i}(E)T_{n}(E)dE=\frac{1}{D}\langle i|T_{n}(\tilde{H})|i\rangle$, and the total (arithmetic average) moments are $\mu_{n}'=\int_{-1}^{1}\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)T_{n}(E)dE=\frac{1}{D}\mathrm{Tr}[T_{n}(\tilde{H})]$.  This KPM formulation and the definition of the moments follow the established KPM procedure. 
[20]

Address truncation and damping of Gibbs oscillations in the Chebyshev expansion: truncate the Chebyshev series at finite order $N$, and apply positive damping (Jackson) factors $g_{n}$ to the moments to obtain the stable numerical estimator
$$
\rho_i(E)=\frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-E^{2}}}\Big[\mu_{0}g_{0}+2\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mu_{n}g_{n}T_{n}(E)\Big],
$$
with
$$
g_{n}=\frac{(N-n+1)\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi n}{N+1}\right)+\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi n}{N+1}\right)\cot\!\left(\frac{\pi}{N+1}\right)}{N+1},
$$
where $N$ is the expansion order. This damping choice is adopted to suppress truncation artifacts (Gibbs oscillations).
[24]
[23]

Explain computational evaluation of the moments and scalability: compute the matrix elements $\langle i|T_{n}(\tilde{H})|i\rangle$ using the Chebyshev recursion on the fly (i.e., propagate $T_{n}(\tilde{H})|i\rangle$ without storing full matrices), and evaluate the trace $\mathrm{Tr}[T_{n}(\tilde{H})]$ stochastically by averaging diagonal matrix elements over random vectors; these strategies reduce memory and CPU requirements and permit treatment of large system sizes.
[20]

Specify the numerical sampling parameters and their rationale used to produce convergent localization diagnostics: select $K_{r}$ as the number of disorder realizations and $K_{s}$ as the number of sampled lattice sites per realization; compute the typical (geometric average) density of states as
$$
\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)=\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{K_{r}K_{s}}\sum_{r=1}^{K_{r}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{s}}\ln\big(\rho_{i}^{r}(E)\big)\right],
$$
and the arithmetic average (total) density of states as
$$
\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)=\frac{1}{K_{r}K_{s}}\sum_{r=1}^{K_{r}}\sum_{i=1}^{K_{s}}\rho_{i}^{r}(E).
$$
In the calculations reported, the authors used $K_{r}=15$ disorder realizations and $K_{s}=15$ sampled sites per realization to obtain stable statistics for $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$.

State the empirical scaling relation between system linear size, expansion order, and spectral resolution used to maintain consistent resolution across sizes: denote the number of lattice sites by $L$ (as reported, system sizes with $L=20\times10^{3}$ to $L=80\times10^{3}$ sites were employed), and choose the expansion order $N$ to scale approximately as $N\sim L^{2}$ so that the energy resolution of the Chebyshev expansion remains adequate when increasing lattice size; the authors explicitly report using $N\sim L^{2}$ and indicate $N=4000$ (and checks up to $N=12000$) for $L=80\times10^{3}$.

Define the localization diagnostic ratio and the finite-size analysis procedure: introduce $R(E)=\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)/\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$ as the dimensionless ratio used to distinguish localized from extended states, note the inequality $R(E)\leq 1$ for all $E$, and perform finite-size scaling by computing $R(E)$ for multiple system sizes ($L=2\times10^{4},4\times10^{4},6\times10^{4},8\times10^{4}$) while monitoring its convergence with increasing $L$ to assess whether observed tendencies persist in the thermodynamic limit.
[26]

Present numerical evidence demonstrating method stability and convergence across disorder strengths: for weak disorder strengths ($W/t=0.5$ and $W/t=1.0$) the computed $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)$ is nonzero and nearly equal to $\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$ across the full bandwidth (indicating extended states), and the four Van-Hove singularities near $E/t\approx\pm1$ and jumps near $E/t\approx\pm3$ appear in the computed $\rho_{\mathrm{av}}(E)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}(E)$ for $L=80\times10^{3}$ and $N=4000$, showing that the KPM reproduces expected spectral features at these sizes and orders; these observations are based on the plotted data comparing average and typical DOS.
Fig. 1

Provide further numerical checks that the KPM-based diagnostics capture localization trends across disorder strengths and are robust to increased expansion order: as disorder strength is increased the typical DOS and the ratio $R(E)$ exhibit the expected suppression patterns (vanishing at band edges first and then across the spectrum for strong disorder), and the finite-size scaling plots of $R(E)$ for energies $E=0$ and $E=0.2$ converge to nearly the same curve for the larger sizes, evidencing that the combination of KPM with the $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}$ versus $\rho_{\mathrm{av}}$ diagnostic yields stable results on the large lattices considered; the authors also checked that increasing $N$ from $4000$ to $12000$ does not appreciably change these results.
Figs. 2, 4, 5

Conclude the operational viability: from the foregoing procedural definitions, numerical parameter choices ($K_{r}=15$, $K_{s}=15$, $L$ up to $8\times10^{4}$ sites, $N\sim L^{2}$), algorithmic elements (rescaled Hamiltonian $\tilde{H}$, Chebyshev moments $\mu_{n}$ and $\mu_{n}'$, Jackson damping $g_{n}$, stochastic trace evaluation), and numerical convergence checks (insensitivity to $N$ increase and finite-size scaling of $R(E)$), assert that the KPM implementation combined with the geometrical versus arithmetic LDOS diagnostic provides an operational and computationally feasible scheme to diagnose extended versus localized single-particle states in disordered bilayer graphene on lattices up to $L=8\times10^{4}$ sites.
[20]

motivating_questions.content: Computationally resolving energy-dependent localization on large two-dimensional bilayer lattices without full diagonalization is challenging because exact diagonalization scales poorly with system size and because distinguishing localized from extended states requires site-resolved spectral information and careful averaging over disorder realizations. Prior to this study, applying KPM to bilayer graphene with the necessary combination of (i) sufficient expansion order, (ii) appropriate damping kernels to control Gibbs oscillations, and (iii) statistical averaging procedures to compute $\rho_{\mathrm{typ}}$ had not been demonstrated at the lattice sizes needed to mitigate finite-size effects. Without a validated, scalable computational protocol, claims about mobility edges and critical disorder strengths could be tainted by numerical artifacts. Establishing and documenting this KPM workflow with concrete numerical parameters addresses the practical obstacle of obtaining reliable LDOS-based localization diagnostics for bilayer graphene.

steps.reasoning:
Define the single-particle density matrix element $\rho_{ij}$ as the integral over energy up to the Fermi energy $E_F$ of the spectral weight connecting basis states $|i\rangle$ and $|j\rangle$, specifically $\rho_{ij} = \int_{-\infty}^{E_F} \langle i|\Psi_k\rangle\langle\Psi_k|j\rangle \delta(E_k - \omega)\,d\omega$, where $|\Psi_k\rangle$ are the eigenfunctions of the Hamiltonian $H$ and $E_k$ are the corresponding eigenenergies; the diagonal element $\rho_{ii}$ is the integrated local density of states. 
[49]

Introduce the spectral function $g_{ij}(\omega)$ as $g_{ij}(\omega) = \sum_k \langle i|\Psi_k\rangle\langle\Psi_k|j\rangle \delta(E_k - \omega)$, and note that $\rho_{ij} = \int_{-\infty}^{E_F} g_{ij}(\omega)\,d\omega$. 
[49]

Express $g_{ij}(\omega)$ in operator form as $g_{ij}(\omega) = \langle i|\delta(H - \omega)|j\rangle$, where $H$ is the sparse tight-binding Hamiltonian of the system and $\delta$ is the Dirac delta function; this expression is the starting point for the kernel polynomial method (KPM). 
[49]

Rescale the Hamiltonian $H$ to $\mathcal{H}$ so that all eigenenergies lie within the interval $(-1,1)$ (this defines the rescaled energy variable denoted again as $\omega$ in the Chebyshev expansion); denote the rescaled Hamiltonian by $\mathcal{H}$ and the rescaled eigenvalues by $\mathcal{E}_k\in(-1,1)$. 
[49]

Expand $g_{ij}(\omega)$ in Chebyshev polynomials $T_n(\omega)$ to obtain the spectral function in the form
$$
g_{ij}(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi\sqrt{1-\omega^2}}\left(\tilde{\mu}_0 + 2\sum_{n=1}^N \tilde{\mu}_n T_n(\omega)\right),
$$
where $\tilde{\mu}_n$ are the modified expansion coefficients for the element $g_{ij}$. 
[49]

Relate the modified coefficients $\tilde{\mu}_n$ to raw coefficients $\mu_n$ via the Jackson kernel as $\tilde{\mu}_n = g_n^N \mu_n$, where the Jackson kernel $g_n^N$ is given by
$$
g_n^N = \frac{(N - n - 1)\cos\left(\frac{\pi n}{N+1}\right) + \sin\left(\frac{\pi n}{N+1}\right)\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{N+1}\right)}{N + 1},
$$
with $N$ the truncation order of the expansion; this kernel improves convergence of the Chebyshev series. 
[49]

Express the raw coefficients $\mu_n$ for two chosen real-space vectors $|v_i\rangle$ and $|v_j\rangle$ (which select basis sites or orbital combinations) as $\mu_n = \langle v_i|T_n(\mathcal{H})|v_j\rangle$, equivalently $\mu_n = \langle v_i|\Psi_k\rangle T_n(\mathcal{E}_k)\langle\Psi_k|v_j\rangle$ after insertion of the spectral decomposition. 
[49]

Compute $\mu_n$ efficiently using recurrence relations for Chebyshev polynomials by defining vectors $|\alpha_n\rangle$ with $|\alpha_0\rangle = |v_i\rangle$, $|\alpha_1\rangle = \mathcal{H}|\alpha_0\rangle$, and the recursion $|\alpha_{n+1}\rangle = 2\mathcal{H}|\alpha_n\rangle - |\alpha_{n-1}\rangle$, and then obtaining $\mu_n$ as the overlap $\mu_n = \langle v_j|\alpha_n\rangle$. These operations involve repeated sparse matrix-vector products with $\mathcal{H}$. 
[49]

Integrate the expanded spectral function $g_{ij}(\omega)$ over energy up to the Fermi level to obtain $\rho_{ij}=\int_{-\infty}^{E_F} g_{ij}(\omega)\,d\omega$, and note that the KPM computes $g_{ij}(\omega)$ for all $\omega$ simultaneously through the same Chebyshev coefficient set, allowing efficient evaluation of the integral for $\rho_{ij}$. 
[49]

Argue that for a sparse tight-binding Hamiltonian the number of nonzero elements scales linearly with system size $N$, and since the KPM computation of the required coefficients only uses sparse matrix-vector products for a fixed, local set of sites, the computational cost to obtain the local $\rho_{ij}$ for a fixed neighborhood scales as $O(N)$ with system size $N$ (i.e., linear scaling), as opposed to full diagonalization which scales as $O(N^3)$. 
[49]

Specify the preprocessing used to convert a local density-matrix block into a fixed-length ANN input vector: choose a local block consisting of a central site and its nearest neighbors; remove redundant entries by discarding the lower triangle of the Hermitian density matrix; concatenate the real parts and imaginary parts of the remaining entries into a one-dimensional array; and append the eigenvalues of the local density matrix to this array to form a fixed-length input vector (the eigenvalues are included as auxiliary, redundant features to aid ANN optimization). Refer to the schematic of this preprocessing and rearrangement. 
Fig. 2

Define the supervised artificial neural network (ANN) classifier architecture: the ANN takes the fixed-length input vector described above and outputs a vector $\vec{v}$ encoding the topological class as a linearly independent target vector (for classification tasks the outputs are encoded as orthogonal vectors so incorrect predictions can be distinguished from false positives); the ANN is trained on translationally invariant (pristine) Hamiltonians with labels given by the corresponding topological invariants calculated in the translationally invariant case. 
Fig. 2

Describe the training and application workflow: (i) generate a training dataset by sampling model Hamiltonian parameters and, for each sample, compute the local density-matrix input (using KPM for large systems or exact diagonalization for small systems) and the corresponding topological invariant for the pristine translationally invariant Hamiltonian (this provides the label); (ii) train the ANN by minimizing a cost function (e.g., squared error) over the dataset to fit the network weights and biases; (iii) apply the trained ANN to local density matrices computed site-by-site in large inhomogeneous or disordered finite systems to obtain a site-resolved prediction of the topological invariant. 
[42]

Conclude that combining (a) the KPM procedure to compute local density-matrix blocks with $O(N)$ scaling for sparse tight-binding Hamiltonians and (b) the trained ANN classifier that maps local density-matrix inputs to topological-class output vectors yields an ANN+KPM pipeline that enables site-resolved evaluation of topological invariants in large systems (tens of thousands of orbitals) without the need for full diagonalization.

motivating_questions.content: Existing exact or momentum-space methods for topological invariants require either full diagonalization of large matrices or knowledge of Bloch wave functions, and therefore have computational complexity that scales superlinearly (e.g., $O(N^3)$ for diagonalization of an $N\times N$ Hamiltonian) and are infeasible for large two-dimensional islands or other big inhomogeneous samples. The kernel polynomial method provides a route to compute local correlation functions and density-matrix elements in linear time for sparse Hamiltonians, but it does not by itself yield a local topological invariant. What is missing is a classification stage that converts locally computed correlation data into a local invariant. The pipeline combining local KPM-computed density matrices with a trained local classifier fills this methodological gap and provides a computationally efficient route to site-resolved topology.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: A computational framework is formulated for electronic-structure calculations of incommensurate layered 2D materials that replaces $k$-space sampling by sampling a compact configuration space $\Omega$ of local relative shifts between layers, and that computes local and global electronic observables from sparse, parameter-free tight-binding Hamiltonians constructed from ab initio DFT–derived Wannier matrix elements. In this framework: $\Omega$ is the two-dimensional toroidal space of relative unit-cell shifts between layers (the "noncommutative Brillouin zone"); for a given configuration $\omega\in\Omega$ a finite circular region (disk) of radius $R$ is built and a sparse Hamiltonian $H^\omega$ is assembled by including all hopping matrix elements $t_{ij}$ within their finite interaction range; local electronic density of states (LEDoS) contributions $g_x(\epsilon)$ and the global EDoS $g(\epsilon)=\sum_x g_x(\epsilon)$ are obtained from $H^\omega$; spectral operators are evaluated efficiently with the kernel polynomial method (KPM) using Chebyshev polynomials $\{T_n\}$ after rescaling the Hamiltonian spectrum to $[-1,1]$; and physical observables are estimated by sampling $\omega$ over $\Omega$ and averaging. The framework is parameter-free with respect to the electronic Hamiltonian (tight-binding hopping terms imported from first-principles Wannier projections) and provides a controllable finite-size error: the finite-disk approximation error decays exponentially with disk radius $R$, enabling systematic convergence to the infinite, aperiodic limit while retaining only sparse matrix-vector operations that are highly parallelizable.

Define the configuration space $\Omega$ as the compact two-dimensional toroidal space of all relative unit-cell shifts between layers (the "noncommutative Brillouin zone"), and denote a particular local relative shift by $\omega\in\Omega$; this space replaces the crystalline Brillouin zone as the sampling domain for incommensurate stacked two-dimensional (2D) layers because translational symmetry of the combined system is absent. 
[14]

Model the electronic structure with a localized-orbital tight-binding description: label localized orbitals by indices $i,j$ and the hopping matrix element between orbitals $i$ and $j$ by $t_{ij}$; form a finite sparse tight-binding Hamiltonian $H$ using these $t_{ij}$ as matrix elements.

Obtain the tight-binding hopping matrix elements $t_{ij}$ from parameter-free first-principles density-functional-theory (DFT) Wannier projections so that the resulting tight-binding Hamiltonian contains no adjustable electronic parameters; denote these DFT-derived Wannier matrix elements as the source of the numerical values of $t_{ij}$.

[19]

For each configuration $\omega\in\Omega$, construct a finite, disk-shaped heterostructure region centered at a reference point with disk radius $R$ (so the finite system contains all orbitals whose positions lie within distance $R$ of the disk center); denote the configuration-dependent sparse Hamiltonian assembled on this disk by $H^{\omega}$.

Assemble $H^{\omega}$ by including only the sparse matrix entries $H_{ij}^{\omega}=t_{ij}$ for orbital pairs $(i,j)$ whose interorbital separation lies within the finite interaction (hopping) range of the DFT-derived $t_{ij}$; this produces a sparse Hamiltonian with a finite number of nonzero entries per row corresponding to the finite hopping range.

Define the local electronic density of states (LEDoS) contribution from orbital $x$ at energy $\epsilon$ as $g_x(\epsilon)$ and the global electronic density of states (EDoS) as the sum over orbitals: $g(\epsilon)=\sum_x g_x(\epsilon)$, where the EDoS is equivalently expressed by summing over eigenstates indexed by $s$ and orbitals $x$ as $g(\epsilon)=\sum_x \frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^N \delta(\epsilon-\epsilon_s)|\phi_s(x)|^2$, with $\{\epsilon_s,\phi_s\}$ the eigenpairs of the finite Hamiltonian.

Evaluate spectral operators, such as the EDoS and LEDoS, efficiently using the kernel polynomial method (KPM): rescale the spectrum of $H^{\omega}$ affinely so all eigenvalues lie in $[-1,1]$, then expand target spectral functions in the basis of Chebyshev polynomials $\{T_n\}$ (where $T_n$ denotes the $n$-th Chebyshev polynomial) and truncate the expansion to compute approximate spectral densities and related operators.

Estimate physical observables of the infinite, aperiodic system by sampling a finite set of configurations $\{\omega\}$ in $\Omega$, computing LEDoS/EDoS (and other operators) for each finite-disk Hamiltonian $H^{\omega}$, and forming configuration-space averages over $\Omega$; this replaces $k$-space sampling with sampling over the configuration space of local relative shifts.

State the finite-disk controllable-error property: because the tight-binding model is local (finite hopping range), the finite-disk truncation error for local observables decays exponentially with the disk radius $R$, so increasing $R$ systematically reduces the finite-size approximation error and allows controlled convergence to the infinite incommensurate limit; this exponential decay and numerical stability are supported by the authors' prior rigorous mathematical analysis.

Emphasize practical implementation details that follow from the framework: (a) construct disk-shaped models of radius $R$ for a chosen reference shift; (b) determine sparse Hamiltonian indices by including only orbital pairs within the finite hopping range; (c) for each configuration $\omega$ displace layers, assemble $H^{\omega}$, and compute LEDoS/EDoS via KPM; (d) sample $\Omega$ with embarrassingly parallel independent configuration computations and average results, while employing optimized multithreaded sparse matrix-vector operations (for example, Intel MKL and MVAPICH) to achieve high parallel efficiency.

Conclude that this computational framework replaces $k$-space sampling with configuration-space $\Omega$ sampling, computes local and global electronic observables from sparse, parameter-free tight-binding Hamiltonians constructed from ab initio Wannier matrix elements, uses finite disks of radius $R$ to assemble $H^{\omega}$ including all $t_{ij}$ within finite interaction range, evaluates spectral operators via KPM/Chebyshev polynomials after rescaling to $[-1,1]$, and estimates physical observables by averaging over $\omega\in\Omega$; the framework is parameter-free with respect to electronic Hamiltonian input and provides a controllable finite-size error that decays exponentially with $R$, while relying only on sparse matrix-vector operations suitable for parallel computation.

motivating_questions.content: In twisted 2D heterostructures one cannot use the conventional crystalline $k$-space approach because the combined system typically lacks a common translational symmetry, so no Brillouin zone or Bloch states exist. Existing remedies — large supercell approximations in DFT or continuum low-energy models — either restrict computations to special commensurate angles (supercells) or introduce uncontrolled approximations and adjustable parameters (phenomenological models). Consequently, there was no general, parameter-free computational strategy that (i) produces EDoS/LEDoS for arbitrary twist angles, (ii) provides controllable finite-size error estimates for convergence to the infinite incommensurate system, and (iii) remains computationally feasible (sparse linear algebra, parallel sampling) for disklike regions large enough to suppress edge effects. A method that trades $k$-space sampling for a configuration-space $\Omega$ sampling and uses ab initio Wannier-derived tight-binding inputs was needed to close this gap.

A computational workflow was implemented that combines the Kubo-Bastin linear-response formula for static susceptibilities,
$\displaystyle \chi_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{O}}=-\frac{2\hbar e}{\Omega}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dE\,F(E)\,\mathrm{ImTr}\big\langle\mathcal{O}\,\partial_{E}G^{+}(E,H)\,v_{\alpha}\,\delta(E-H)\big\rangle,$
with an exact real-space expression for the symmetrized itinerant orbital operator given by the Green-function integral representation
$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Mod}}=-\frac{i e \hbar^{2} \varepsilon_{\alpha \beta \gamma}}{4 g_{L} \mu_{B}} \int d E & {\left[\operatorname{Re}\left(G^{+}(E, H)\right) v_{\alpha} \delta(H-E) v_{\beta}\right.} \\
& \left.+v_{\alpha} \delta(H-E) v_{\beta} \operatorname{Re}\left(G^{-}(E, H)\right)\right],
\end{aligned}
$$
and the kernel polynomial method (KPM) Chebyshev expansion of Green's functions to perform large-scale, real-space calculations. This combined scheme enables efficient, unbiased computation of itinerant OAM, ACA OAM, and spin susceptibilities in tight-binding models of isolated 2D TMDs and realistic TMD/ferromagnet heterostructures, including the possibility of treating disorder and spatially resolved projections onto specific layers or sites.

steps.reasoning:
Present the static linear-response expression used to compute spin and orbital susceptibilities: the susceptibility $\chi_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{O}}$ (change in the expectation of operator $\mathcal{O}$ due to an electric field applied along direction $\alpha$) is given by the Kubo-Bastin kernel
$$
\chi_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{O}}=-\frac{2\hbar e}{\Omega}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dE\,F(E)\,\mathrm{ImTr}\big\langle\mathcal{O}\,\partial_{E}G^{+}(E,H)\,v_{\alpha}\,\delta(E-H)\big\rangle,
$$
where $\Omega$ is the sample volume, $F(E)=(\exp((E-\mu)/K_{\mathrm{B}}T)+1)^{-1}$ is the Fermi-Dirac distribution with chemical potential $\mu$ and temperature $T$, $G^{\pm}(E,H)=[E-H\pm i0^{+}]^{-1}$ are the retarded/advanced Green's functions for Hamiltonian $H$, $v_{\alpha}\equiv\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,r_{\alpha}]$ is the $\alpha$-component of the velocity operator with $r_{\alpha}$ the position operator, and $\mathcal{O}$ denotes the operator whose linear-response is sought (for example, out-of-plane orbital $L_{z}$ or spin $S_{z}$).
[53]

Provide the exact real-space Green-function representation used for the symmetrized itinerant orbital angular momentum operator $L_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Mod}}$ (this operator captures itinerant, inter-site contributions rather than atom-centered moments): 
$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Mod}}=-\frac{i e \hbar^{2} \varepsilon_{\alpha \beta \gamma}}{4 g_{L} \mu_{B}} \int d E & {\left[\operatorname{Re}\left(G^{+}(E, H)\right) v_{\alpha} \delta(H-E) v_{\beta}\right.} \\
& \left.+v_{\alpha} \delta(H-E) v_{\beta} \operatorname{Re}\left(G^{-}(E, H)\right)\right],
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta\gamma}$ is the Levi-Civita tensor, $g_{L}$ is the orbital Landé $g$-factor, and $\mu_{B}$ is the Bohr magneton; this representation expresses the off-diagonal position-operator matrix elements via Green functions and thus yields an exact real-space description of the itinerant OAM operator appropriate for disordered and finite systems.
[51]

State that the Green functions appearing in the above expressions are expanded using the kernel polynomial method (KPM) via Chebyshev polynomial series to enable efficient large-scale, real-space numerical evaluation: the KPM expansion approximates $G^{\pm}(E,H)$ (and related spectral kernels such as $\delta(H-E)$ and $\operatorname{Re}G^{\pm}$) as finite Chebyshev series, allowing scalable computation of the traces and energy integrals in the Kubo-Bastin expression and in the itinerant $L_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Mod}}$ expression for large tight-binding Hamiltonians.
[52]

Combine the prior elements into a computational workflow: (i) evaluate the itinerant orbital operator $L_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Mod}}$ in its exact real-space Green-function integral form (previous step), (ii) compute the Kubo-Bastin susceptibility kernel for the operator of interest $\mathcal{O}$ by inserting the evaluated operator and the KPM-expanded Green-function and spectral-operator representations, and (iii) perform the energy integrals and traces numerically in real space using the Chebyshev expansions and stochastic trace techniques to obtain $\chi_{\alpha}^{\mathcal{O}}$ for large tight-binding systems.
[51]

Define the practical outputs and capabilities of this scheme: it yields unbiased, real-space-resolved numerical values for itinerant OAM densities (via $L^{\mathrm{Mod}}$), atom-centered (ACA) OAM densities (via the matrix elements of $L_{z}$ in the atomic orbital basis), and spin susceptibilities (via $\mathcal{O}=S_{z}$) in tight-binding models; the method naturally accommodates disorder and enables spatial projections onto layers or specific sites, which is essential to analyze isolated two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) and TMD/ferromagnet heterostructures on the same footing.

motivating_questions.content: The scientific need was for a numerically efficient, real-space approach capable of resolving itinerant orbital effects and their spatial projection in large heterostructures and disordered samples. Prior Kubo/eigenstate formulations or ACA-only treatments could not simultaneously (i) represent the itinerant OAM operator in a form suitable for projection onto real-space sites and interfaces, (ii) be applied to large tight-binding heterostructures with hybridization and spatial inhomogeneity, and (iii) be efficiently evaluated numerically for dense energy resolution. Without such a scheme, quantitative predictions of interface imprinting, spatially resolved susceptibilities, and the role of disorder or finite-size effects were inaccessible.

reasoning_chains.conclusion_text: The study demonstrates a multiscale, parameter-free workflow that: (i) extracts an effective, non-orthogonal tight-binding Hamiltonian and overlap for the carbon $\pi$-system directly from converged DFT Hamiltonian and overlap matrices using the SISL utility; (ii) employs the DFT-parameterized tight-binding model in large-scale Green's-function transport calculations with TBtrans to compute transmission and bond-current maps for supercells containing up to 345,920 atoms and device areas up to approximately $80\\ \\mathrm{nm} \\times 160\\ \\mathrm{nm}$; and (iii) simulates localized current injection via a single-atom localized on-site broadening self-energy $i\\Gamma$ (with $\\Gamma$ chosen as $1\\ \\mathrm{eV}$ for these demonstrations), together with complex absorbing potentials to avoid spurious reflections. This workflow yields DFT-grounded transport predictions at the 10^2 nm scale without employing empirical tunable parameters in the TB parametrization.

The paper states these tools and definitions when introducing the multiscale workflow used throughout the study. 
[18]

State that the DFT electronic structure and converged DFT Hamiltonian and overlap matrices are obtained with the SIESTA DFT implementation, using a single-$\zeta$ basis (for planar structures), norm-conserving pseudopotentials, a specified k-point sampling, and structural relaxation to a 0.01 eV/Å force threshold; these converged Hamiltonian and overlap matrices are the starting DFT data used for subsequent model extraction.

Explain the procedure to extract an effective tight-binding model from the DFT matrices: SISL is used to extract an effective, non-orthogonal tight-binding Hamiltonian and overlap that retain the interaction range of the DFT basis and include all on-site and coupling elements associated with the carbon $p_z$ orbitals (for planar NPG), or $s,p_x,p_y,p_z$ orbitals for non-planar conformations; this produces a DFT-parameterized TB model that explicitly includes the overlap matrix and DFT-derived coupling elements and thus contains no empirically tuned TB parameters.

[20]

Describe how localized injection is implemented in the device-scale transport simulations: injection is modelled by adding a constant, on-site level broadening self-energy $i\Gamma$ localized on a single atom (the authors use $\Gamma = 1\\ \\mathrm{eV}$), which is equivalent to modelling an STM tip injecting electrons at that atomic site; the value of $\Gamma$ acts mainly as a scaling factor for injected currents and is chosen arbitrarily for demonstration.

Explain the treatment of device boundaries and avoidance of spurious reflections: the left and right extremes of the finite device along the transverse direction are equipped with 5 nm wide regions that implement complex absorbing potentials (CAP) to absorb outgoing waves and thereby avoid electronic back-reflection at non-periodic walls in the large-scale device calculations.

Summarize the key claim about parameter-freeness: because the TB Hamiltonian and overlap are extracted directly from converged DFT Hamiltonian and overlap matrices (no fitted or empirical TB parameters are introduced) and the transport calculations use that DFT-parameterized TB model with physically defined injection ($i\Gamma$) and CAP boundary conditions, the workflow provides DFT-grounded transport predictions at the $10^{2}\\ \\mathrm{nm}$ scale without employing empirical tunable parameters in the TB parametrization.

motivating_questions.content: Quantitative, atomically resolved transport predictions for candidate NPG designs at device-relevant (>10 nm) length scales are computationally challenging because direct DFT-based transport scales prohibitively with system size. Prior reduced models either lacked DFT grounding or could not address system sizes required to observe Talbot spreading and long-range confinement. There was therefore a methodological gap: a parameter-free route to carry DFT electronic structure information into tractable, accurate large-scale quantum transport simulations that can validate chemical-design ideas (para/meta bridging) at 100 nm scales. Closing this gap is necessary to provide predictive guidance for experiments and device design.

premises.content: The KPM implementation uses a Gaussian kernel broadening of width \(\sigma \approx 5\) meV (from \(p=4000\) Chebyshev moments). For small twist angles (e.g., \(\theta < 2^\circ\)), the predicted bandwidth of moiré flat bands can be sub-meV, making these features poorly resolved or invisible in the KPM LDoS. For MoS\(_2\) at \(4^\circ\), the flat bands are "barely resolved". At the critical twist angles of approximately \(4.6^\circ\) (\(n=0\)), \(3.5^\circ\) (\(n=1\)), and \(2.8^\circ\) (\(n=2\)), the bandwidth is at most 5 meV, so they may be seen at the edge of resolution.

premises.content: Two concurrent implementations for quasi-eigenstate (QE) computation are provided. (i) QE-Concurrent-S (state-based) reconstructs the intermediate states \(|\psi(\pm t_j)\rangle\) from stored Chebyshev vectors \(\{T_n(\tilde{H})|\psi\rangle\}\) with memory scaling as \(O(N_{\mathrm{basis}} \cdot b)\), where \(N_{\mathrm{basis}}\) is the basis-set size and \(b\) the block size. It achieves a measured peak speedup of \(\approx 3.3\times\) at \(b \approx 40\) with a memory overhead of \(\sim 16\%\) for \(N_t = 1024\). (ii) QE-Concurrent-E (energy-based) directly computes quasi-eigenstates \(|\Psi(E)\rangle = \sum_{n=0}^{N(\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{tot}})} C_n^{\mathrm{QE}}(E) T_n(\tilde{H})|\psi\rangle\) using energy-dependent coefficients \(C_n^{\mathrm{QE}}(E) = \tau\sum_{j=N_0}^{N_t} \frac{(2-\delta_{j,0})}{2}( \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}E t_j} c_n(\tilde{t}_j) + \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}E t_j} c_n(-\tilde{t}_j) )\), requires no extra memory when the number of sampled energies \(N_E\) is small, and attains \(\sim 9\)–\(10\times\) speedup for \(N_E = 5\). Accuracy against the sequential QE method is excellent: the infinity-norm error is below \(1.3\times10^{-17}\) for both implementations.

The moment-based EC-Concurrent-M computes the Chebyshev moments \(m_{n,\alpha}^{\mathrm{EC}}(E) = \langle\psi_{1,\alpha}^{\mathrm{EC}}|T_n(\tilde{H})|\psi_{2,\alpha}^{\mathrm{EC}}(E)\rangle\) during a single long-time propagation and reconstructs the correlation function as

The state-based EC-Concurrent-S (with optimal block size \(b \approx 40\)) reaches a measured speedup of \(\approx 3.5\times\) with \(\sim 11\%\) memory overhead, while EC-Concurrent-M approaches the propagation-part limit of \(\sim 6\times\) and outperforms EC-Concurrent-S for small numbers of sampled energies \(N_E\) (crossover around \(N_E \approx 200\)).
